props.title: When We Leave
props.initialSlug: Woman flees Turkish family to escape honor killing

sections.content: When We Leave (2010) stands as one of the most powerful examinations of honor killings and cultural displacement in contemporary cinema. Director Feo Aladag crafts a devastating portrait of Umay, a Turkish-German woman who flees an abusive marriage in Istanbul to return to her family in Berlin. The film shares thematic DNA with Fatih Akin's Head-On (2004) and The Edge of Heaven (2007), exploring the complex intersection of Turkish and German cultures. What sets When We Leave apart is its unflinching look at how traditional values can become weapons of oppression.

sections.content: The film connects to a broader cinematic examination of women's rights and cultural identity in Muslim communities, seen in works like Persepolis (2007) and Wadjda (2012). These films share a common thread of female protagonists pushing against patriarchal structures while maintaining deep connections to their cultural heritage. Director Aladag's background in domestic violence advocacy brings authenticity to the portrayal of systematic oppression, making the film particularly resonant with other works addressing honor-based violence like In the Name of the Father (1993). SUBHEAD: Cultural Identity and Displacement

The film's exploration of displacement and belonging echoes through other powerful works like In This World (2002) and The Other Side of Hope (2017). Sibel Kekilli's devastating performance as Umay captures the impossible choice between personal freedom and family loyalty. The film's visual language, particularly its use of confined spaces and surveillance-style shots, creates a mounting sense of claustrophobia that recalls 4 Months, 3 Weeks and 2 Days (2007) in its portrayal of systemic oppression.
